docs.title: CaloCem
docs.text:
CaloCem reads, plots and analyses isothermal heat flow calorimetry data, with a focus on the hydration of cementitious materials. It loads the exports of TAM Air calorimeters, combines many experiments in one pandas DataFrame and extracts characteristic values such as cumulative heat, peak positions, the dormant period and the slope of the main hydration peak.

Warning

CaloCem has been developed without involvement of TA Instruments and is thus independent from the company and its software.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
CaloCem requires Python 3.10 or newer and is available on PyPI:

pip install calocem

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Put the exported .csv or .xls files of your experiments into one folder, e.g. calo_data, next to your script:

.
├── myscript.py
└── calo_data
    ├── opc_1.csv
    └── opc_2.csv

Load and plot the data:

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from calocem import Measurement, ProcessingParameters

datapath = Path(__file__).parent / "calo_data"
tam = Measurement(folder=datapath, show_info=False)

ax = tam.plot(t_unit="h")
ax.set_xlim(0, 48)
plt.show()

The data of all samples is available as a DataFrame:

data = tam.get_data()
print(tam.get_sample_names())

Analysis settings are collected in ProcessingParameters and passed to the analysis methods, which return DataFrames with one row per sample:

processparams = ProcessingParameters()
processparams.cutoff.cutoff_min = 30  # ignore the first 30 minutes

peaks = tam.get_peaks(processparams, show_plot=False)
mainpeak = tam.get_mainpeak_params(processparams)

print(mainpeak[["sample_short", "gradient_from_max_slope", "onset_time_min_max_slope"]])

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Measurement.get_heat_between(start_s, end_s) returns the heat released between two times. The limits can be one time for all samples or one time per sample (dict or pd.Series keyed by sample_short), e.g. the onset from get_mainpeak_params().

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Measurement.apply_tian_correction() without processparams crashed with an AttributeError; it now uses the instance's parameters.
  • Measurement.get_ascending_flank_tangent() crashed because it called a removed method. It works again, and flank_fraction_start, flank_fraction_end, window_size and cutoff_min override the corresponding processparams values.
  • regex was dropped by the maximum-slope analysis, so get_maximum_slope(), get_mainpeak_params() and get_peak_onset_via_max_slope() returned max-slope results for all samples.
  • Measurement.plot_by_category() was an empty stub; it again yields one plot per metadata group, as documented.
  • PlottingParameters.plot_title is now a proper dataclass field and can be passed to the constructor.
  • calocem no longer changes matplotlib's font settings. Importing it used to set the global font.family to serif; plots now use your matplotlib style.
  • Plots: get_peaks marks the peaks in the color of each curve, without a file path in the title or repeated legend entries; get_astm_c1679_characteristics shows one legend entry for the ASTM markers; the main peak plot of get_mainpeak_params no longer shows the maximum slope point twice, labels the y axis correctly (W g⁻¹), and shows the dormant heat flow and the gradient in the selected heat unit instead of rounding the former to 0.
  • Exceptions re-raised by calocem now chain the original error (raise ... from e).

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text:
• Measurement.get_cumulated_heat_at_hours() is renamed to get_cumulative_heat_at_hours(), and its result column cumulated_heat_at_hours to cumulative_heat_j_g. The old method emits a DeprecationWarning; the old column is still included.
  • Arguments that had no effect now emit a DeprecationWarning when passed: get_dormant_period_heatflow(cutoff_min, prominence, plot_right_boundary, show_plot), get_peak_onsets(show_plot, ax), get_maximum_slope(save_path, xunit), get_average_slope(save_path, xunit), get_peak_onset_via_max_slope(time_discarded_s, save_path, xscale, xunit, intersection), get_astm_c1679_characteristics(xscale), get_ascending_flank_tangent(show_plot, plotpath, ax) and Measurement(new_code). Use ProcessingParameters instead.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• Internal plotting helpers that could no longer run (SimplePlotter.plot_flank_tangent, SimplePlotter.plot_onset_intersections and their private Measurement callers).
  • Unused requests dependency.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Restructured the documentation: new quickstart on the home page, new pages Loading Data and Processing Parameters, revised Characteristic Values, Plotting and Tian Correction pages. The outdated how-to guide was merged into these pages.
  • The reference now covers ProcessingParameters and all parameter groups; the public Measurement methods have numpy-style docstrings listing parameters, returned columns and units.
  • Fixed the Tian correction docs: a single time constant requires tau2 = None.
  • Added a changelog page and a quickstart to the README.
  • The figures of Characteristic Values are generated from the current code by scripts/make_doc_figures.py; an ASTM C1679 figure was added.
  • The main peak example on Characteristic Values uses smoothing_1st_deriv = 1e-13; the former 1e-12 underestimated the maximum slope by about 40 %.

docs.title: Internal
docs.text:
• CI now runs ruff and mypy; both pass. The example scripts are run in CI.
  • Replaced two test scripts that swallowed exceptions with real tests.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Measurement.save(path) and Measurement.load(path). Persist a processed Measurement to a single, user-named pickle file and restore it in a downstream script. The whole object is stored, so processed (e.g. downsampled) data, info, added metadata and processparams are all preserved. This is a convenience cache, not an archive — the raw source files remain the source of truth, and a file that fails to load can be regenerated by re-running from the original folder. The .pkl extension is recommended to keep the format explicit.
m = Measurement(folder, processparams=processparams)
m.save("run01.pkl")

# later, in another script
m = Measurement.load("run01.pkl")
  • Measurement.get_data_with_metadata(). Returns the measurement data joined with its added metadata as one tidy DataFrame, ready to export with .to_csv(...). Works on per-sample data (joining on the metadata id column) and after average_by_metadata (joining on the group label and attaching only metadata that is constant within each group). Returns the data unchanged when no metadata has been added.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • DownSamplingParameters.smoothing_factor is now scale-relative. It is scaled internally by the number of points and the heat-flow variance instead of being passed to the spline as an absolute residual target, so the same value behaves consistently regardless of heat-flow magnitude. The default changed from 1e-10 to 1e-6. This changes which points adaptive downsampling selects.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Adaptive downsampling works again. Measurement(..., processparams=pp) with pp.downsample.apply = True had silently returned the full-resolution data since the package refactor, because _apply_adaptive_downsampling was left as a no-op stub. It now downsamples per sample as documented.
  • UnivariateSpline "s too small" warning removed. The spline fit during downsampling no longer emits a non-convergence UserWarning.

docs.title: Breaking Changes
docs.text:
• Pickle caching is now opt-in. Measurement(folder=...) no longer writes _data.pickle and _info.pickle to the working directory by default. Pass save_cache=True explicitly to enable it.

Migrate:

# old (implicit caching)
m = Measurement(folder)

# new — equivalent caching behavior
m = Measurement(folder, save_cache=True)

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • save_cache: bool = False kwarg on Measurement.__init__. Controls whether pickle cache files are written when loading from a folder. The existing cold_start=False read path is unchanged.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• New tutorial notebook docs/example_get_mainpeak_params.ipynb walking through get_mainpeak_params, with notebooks executed at docs build time so outputs stay in sync with the code.
  • Replaced stale TAInstCalorimetry references and corrected the package name and PyPI URL across docs/index.md, docs/how-to-guide.md, docs/quantification.md, and docs/tian.md.

docs.title: Internal
docs.text:
• Notebooks are now exercised under pytest via nbmake so doc examples cannot silently rot.
  • nbstripout configured to keep notebook diffs clean.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • CSV files with a trailing comments column (e.g. annotations like "experiment interrupted and restarted") are now parsed correctly.

docs.title: Breaking Changes
docs.text:
• calocem.tacalorimetry has been removed. The legacy monolithic Measurement implementation (tacalorimetry.py, ~3 400 lines) has been retired. The module now exists as a stub that raises a FutureWarning on import and forwards to the refactored implementation. The old and new implementations are not guaranteed to produce identical numerical results. Users who require the previous behaviour should pin to calocem<0.3.0.

Migrate your imports:

# old
from calocem.tacalorimetry import Measurement

# new — preferred
from calocem import Measurement

# new — explicit
from calocem.measurement import Measurement

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Public package API. Measurement and ProcessingParameters are now importable directly from the top-level package: 
    from calocem import Measurement, ProcessingParameters

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Eliminated all pandas Copy-on-Write FutureWarning and DeprecationWarning occurrences triggered by chained assignment patterns in utils.py and tacalorimetry.py. The package is now silent on pandas 2.x and compatible with the Copy-on-Write behaviour that becomes the default in pandas 3.0.
  • float() called on a single-element Series replaced with float(series.iloc[0]) to silence pandas DeprecationWarning.
  • Removed stray print("hallo") debug statement from the data loading path.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• ipykernel moved to dev dependencies — it is no longer installed as part of a normal pip install calocem. Users who need it for notebooks should install it explicitly (pip install ipykernel).
  • Replaced logging.basicConfig() call at import time with a module-level logger. CaloCem no longer writes CaloCem.log to the working directory on import or hijacks the host application's log configuration.

docs.title: Internal
docs.text:
• /.cache added to .gitignore to stop the mkdocs-git-committers cache from being tracked.
  • Manual exploration scripts (script_test_*.py) moved from tests/ to examples/ where the other example scripts live. They are not pytest tests and were silently collected without asserting anything.
  • Removed unused live import pysnooper from tests/test_read_calo_data_xls.py.
• See repository history for changes prior to this changelog.

docs.title: Extracting Main-Peak Parameters¶
docs.text:
In isothermal heat-flow calorimetry of cementitious materials, the main hydration peak (driven by the silicate reaction) is characterized by parameters such as the maximum slope, the mean slope of the ascending flank, and the times at which these features occur.

Measurement.get_mainpeak_params() extracts these parameters in a single call and returns them in a pandas.DataFrame. Two analysis modes are available:

  • method="mean" (default) — combines a maximum-slope and a mean-slope (flank-tangent) analysis.
  • method="ascending" — uses a first-ascending-slope-to-fraction approach, which can be more robust for noisy or asymmetric peaks.

This tutorial walks through both, starting from a minimal call and progressively customizing the processing parameters.

docs.title: A minimal call¶
docs.text: Without any custom processing parameters, get_mainpeak_params() runs both the maximum-slope and mean-slope analyses on the loaded sample. Setting show_plot=True and plot_type="mean" produces a flank-tangent visualization alongside the returned DataFrame.

docs.title: Customizing the processing¶
docs.text:
Real calorimetry data is rarely clean enough for the defaults to give the best result. Three groups of ProcessingParameters typically matter for slope analysis:

  • Smoothing — median_filter removes single-point noise; spline_interpolation smooths the first and second derivatives, which the slope detection relies on.
  • Cutoff — cutoff.cutoff_min discards the early measurement period (mixing artefacts, thermal equilibration) so they don't bias the analysis.
  • Flank fraction — slope_analysis.flank_fraction_start/_end define which portion of the ascending flank counts as "the slope" for the mean-slope (flank-tangent) analysis.

docs.title: Alternative analysis: method="ascending"¶
docs.text:
For noisy or asymmetric peaks, where a symmetric flank fit struggles, the first-ascending-slope-to-fraction approach can be more robust. Instead of fitting a tangent to a defined fraction of the flank, the algorithm walks up the rising heat-flow signal until it reaches a target fraction of the peak maximum (or a target heat-flow delta) and returns the slope of that ascent.

The next example switches to the flank_detection3 dataset, which is well-suited to demonstrating this analysis, and uses parameters tuned for first-ascending detection.

docs.title: Closing notes¶
docs.text:
Inspect mainpeak_custom.columns or mainpeak_ascending.columns to see the full set of values returned for your data — many additional intermediate quantities are available alongside the slopes and timestamps.

Further customization is available through ProcessingParameters.plotting (figure size, axis limits, legend position, plot titles drawn from metadata columns, monochrome styling) and through save_plot=True / plotpath=... for batch plot export. Sample-specific parameter overrides are supported via processparams.add_sample_param_rule(regex, {...}).

Related methods for other aspects of the heat-flow signal:

  • Measurement.get_peaks() — peak detection across the full time series.
  • Measurement.get_peak_onsets() — gradient-threshold-based onset detection.
  • Measurement.get_maximum_slope() — maximum-slope detection only, without the combined output.

docs.title: Loading a folder
docs.text:
A Measurement reads all supported files of one folder (not its subfolders):

from pathlib import Path
from calocem import Measurement

datapath = Path(__file__).parent / "calo_data"

tam = Measurement(folder=datapath, show_info=True)

With show_info=True the name of each file is printed while it is read. Files that cannot be read are skipped with a warning.

To load only some files, pass a regular expression. It is matched against the beginning of the file name:

tam = Measurement(folder=datapath, regex=r"opc_.*\.csv")

docs.title: Supported files
docs.text: Export Extension Notes TAM Air CSV export .csv The usual comma-separated export. A Reaction start time is used as time zero; periods between Experiment interrupted and Experiment restarted are removed. TAM Air Excel export .xls Requires a sheet named Raw data; sample information is read from SampleData. .xlsx files are not loaded. First-generation tab-separated export .csv Heat flow in mW with decimal commas; the sample mass is read from the file and the heat is integrated. Data previously processed by CaloCem .csv Load with processed=True, e.g. a file written with tam.get_data().to_csv(...).

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
get_data() returns all samples in one pandas DataFrame in long format, i.e. one row per sample and time:

data = tam.get_data()
Column Unit Description time_s s Time since the start of the reaction. temperature_c °C Temperature (not available for all exports). heat_flow_w W Measured heat flow. heat_j J Cumulated heat. normalized_heat_flow_w_g W/g Heat flow per gram of sample. normalized_heat_j_g J/g Cumulated heat per gram of sample. sample Full path of the source file. sample_short File name without extension, used as sample name.

get_sample_names() lists the sample names, get_information() returns the sample information stored in the files (e.g. the sample mass).

Some exports contain differently named temperature columns. Pass auto_clean=True to merge them into temperature_c and to drop rows without heat flow values.

If the mass stored in a file is wrong, the normalized columns can be recalculated for one sample:

tam.normalize_sample_to_mass("opc_1", mass_g=6.05)

docs.title: Adding metadata
docs.text:
Information about the samples, e.g. cement type or water-to-cement ratio, is usually kept in a separate table. Add it as CSV or Excel file with one row per sample and a column that contains the sample names (the file names without extension):

experiment_nr,date,cement_name,cement_amount_g,water_amount_g
calorimetry_data_1,01.01.2023,cem_a,100,50
calorimetry_data_2,01.01.2023,cem_b,100,40

tam = Measurement(
    folder=datapath,
    metadata_path="metadata.csv",
    metadata_id_column="experiment_nr",
)
# or, for an existing Measurement
tam.add_metadata_source("metadata.csv", "experiment_nr")

The metadata is used for plot titles, for plotting by category and for averaging. get_data_with_metadata() returns the data with the metadata columns joined to every row, which is convenient for plotting with libraries such as seaborn.

docs.title: Averaging replicates
docs.text:
Samples that share the same metadata values can be averaged. The heat flow and heat of every sample are interpolated onto a common time grid (bin_width_s, default 60 s), then mean and standard deviation are computed per group:

tam.average_by_metadata("cement_name")
tam.plot()  # one curve per cement

tam.undo_average_by_metadata()  # back to the individual samples

The averaged data contains the columns time_s, heat_flow_w, heat_j, normalized_heat_flow_w_g, normalized_heat_j_g, each with a matching *_std column, and the group name in sample and sample_short. Other columns, e.g. the temperature, are dropped. All analysis methods then work on the averaged curves.

docs.title: Downsampling
docs.text:
Files with many data points slow down the analysis. Adaptive downsampling keeps more points where the curve changes and fewer in flat regions. It is enabled through the processing parameters and applied when the Measurement is created:

from calocem import ProcessingParameters

processparams = ProcessingParameters()
processparams.downsample.apply = True
processparams.downsample.num_points = 2000

tam = Measurement(folder=datapath, processparams=processparams)

docs.title: Saving and reloading
docs.text:
Reading and processing many files takes time. A Measurement can be saved to a file and restored in another script:

tam.save("processed_run.pkl")

# later
tam = Measurement.load("processed_run.pkl")

The whole object is stored: data, information, metadata and processing parameters. The file is a convenience cache, not an archive. Files written by an incompatible CaloCem version cannot be loaded; recreate them from the original data.

Older cache files

Measurement(..., save_cache=True) writes _data.pickle and _info.pickle to the current working directory, and Measurement(folder, cold_start=False) reads them back. save() and load() are the recommended replacement, since they use a file name of your choice. remove_pickle_files() deletes the old cache files.

docs.title: Plotting¶
docs.text:
The Measurement object loads all calorimetry files of a folder. Its plot method draws the heat flow (or any other data column) of all samples into one figure and returns the Matplotlib axes, which can then be customized with the usual Matplotlib methods.

This page is a Jupyter notebook that is executed when the documentation is built, so all plots below are generated from the example data in the repository.

docs.title: Choosing what to plot¶
docs.text:
plot accepts

  • y: the column to plot, e.g. "normalized_heat_flow_w_g" (default) or "normalized_heat_j_g",
  • t_unit: the time unit, "s", "min", "h" (default) or "d",
  • y_unit_milli: show the y-values in mW/g or mJ/g instead of W/g or J/g (default True),
  • regex: plot only the samples whose name matches,
  • ax: an existing Matplotlib axes to draw into.

docs.title: Heat flow and heat in subplots¶
docs.text: Because plot draws into a given axes, several views can be combined. Here, the early reaction and the main hydration period are shown for both the heat flow and the cumulated heat.

docs.title: Heat flow with its gradient¶
docs.text: plot_heatflow_with_gradient adds the time derivative of the heat flow on a second y-axis and returns both axes. This is useful to check the smoothing settings before running a slope analysis (see Processing Parameters).

docs.title: Plotting by metadata category¶
docs.text: If metadata is attached, plot_by_category creates one figure per value of one or more metadata columns. It is a generator that yields the category value and the axes of each figure.

docs.title: Processing Parameters
docs.text:
All analysis settings in CaloCem live in one object, ProcessingParameters. You create it once, change the values you need and pass it to the methods of Measurement:

from calocem import Measurement, ProcessingParameters

processparams = ProcessingParameters()
processparams.cutoff.cutoff_min = 30
processparams.spline_interpolation.apply = True

tam = Measurement(folder="calo_data", processparams=processparams)
peaks = tam.get_peaks(processparams, show_plot=False)

If a method is called without processparams, it uses the parameters the Measurement was created with (or the defaults).

The parameters are grouped by topic. Each group is a small dataclass, so you can also create a group directly, e.g. ProcessingParameters(cutoff=CutOffParameters(cutoff_min=30)).

docs.title: cutoff
docs.text:
The beginning of a measurement is usually disturbed by mixing and thermal equilibration. cutoff_min removes it from the analysis.

Field Default Description cutoff_min 60 Time in minutes. Data with time_s < cutoff_min * 60 is ignored. 0 disables the cutoff.

cutoff_min is honoured by peak detection, dormant period, maximum and mean slope, first ascending slope, deconvolution and the related plots.

Exceptions

  • get_cumulative_heat_at_hours does not discard data; instead, the heat released up to cutoff_min is subtracted from the heat at target_h.
  • get_peak_onsets ignores cutoff_min and uses its own time_discarded_s argument.
  • The half-maximum search of get_astm_c1679_characteristics uses the unfiltered data; only the peak detection it relies on honours the cutoff.

docs.title: time_constants
docs.text:
Time constants of the calorimeter for the Tian correction, in seconds. Used by apply_tian_correction only.

Field Default Description tau1 300 First time constant. tau2 100 Second time constant. Set to None to correct with tau1 only.

docs.title: peakdetection
docs.text:
Passed to scipy.signal.find_peaks when searching peaks in the heat flow.

Field Default Description prominence 1e-5 Minimum peak prominence, in the unit of the analysed column (W/g). Decrease it to find smaller peaks. distance 100 Minimum distance between peaks as a number of data points, not a time.

Peak detection is the first step of get_peaks, get_dormant_period_heatflow, get_astm_c1679_characteristics and get_mainpeak_params.

docs.title: Smoothing
docs.text:
Derivatives of measured heat flow are noisy. Three groups control smoothing. They act at different points, so it matters which analysis you run:

Group Fields (default) What is smoothed rolling_mean apply (False), window (11 points) Heat flow, before the gradient is taken. Used by the maximum slope analysis and plot_heatflow_with_gradient. median_filter apply (False), size (7 points) The first and second derivative of the heat flow (not the heat flow itself). spline_interpolation apply (False), smoothing_1st_deriv (1e-9), smoothing_2nd_deriv (1e-9) A cubic smoothing spline is fitted to the first and second derivative. The values are passed as s to UnivariateSpline; larger values mean smoother curves.

The smoothed derivatives are used by the maximum slope analysis (get_maximum_slope, get_mainpeak_params, get_peak_onset_via_max_slope), plot_heatflow_with_gradient and apply_tian_correction. The mean slope, first ascending slope, peak detection and deconvolution work on the unsmoothed data.

docs.title: downsample
docs.text:
Large files can be thinned out when the Measurement is created. Points are kept preferentially where the heat flow curve bends, so peaks stay sharp while flat regions are thinned out. Values are picked from the measured data, not interpolated.

Field Default Description apply False Enable downsampling. num_points 1000 Target number of points per sample (an upper bound). smoothing_factor 1e-6 Smoothing of the spline used to estimate the curvature. baseline_weight 0.1 Share of points spread evenly, so flat regions are not emptied. section_split False Downsample the data before and after section_split_time_s separately. section_split_time_s 1000 Split time in seconds.

Downsampling only takes effect when passed to the constructor: Measurement(folder, processparams=processparams). Save the result with tam.save(...) to avoid repeating it, see Loading data.

docs.title: slope_analysis
docs.text:
Controls the analyses of the main hydration peak, see Main Peak Parameters.

Field Default Description flank_fraction_start 0.35 Start of the ascending flank, as fraction of the height between the minimum before the peak and the peak. flank_fraction_end 0.55 End of the ascending flank, same scale. window_size 0.1 Width of the averaging window for the mean slope, as fraction of the time span of the flank. first_ascending_fraction_of_max 0.2 method="ascending": heat flow threshold as fraction of the maximum (after cutoff). Must be in (0, 1]. first_ascending_range_method "fraction" method="ascending": "fraction" uses the flank fractions above, "delta" uses a fixed heat-flow rise. first_ascending_delta_y_w_g 0.001 "delta" mode: rise of the heat flow in W/g that defines the segment. flexible 0.0 "delta" mode: widens the delta for high peaks; 0 disables it.

docs.title: deconvolution
docs.text:
Used by get_deconvolution and get_left_peak_inflection_tangent_intersection, which fit a sum of peaks plus a baseline to the heat flow.

Field Default Description n_peaks 2 Number of peaks to fit. baseline_mode "constant" "constant", "linear", "chebyshev" or "none". chebyshev_degree 2 Polynomial degree for baseline_mode="chebyshev". max_nfev 5000 Maximum number of optimizer iterations. max_fit_points 2500 The data is subsampled to at most this many points for the fit. min_points 30 Samples with fewer points (after cutoff) are skipped. min_peak_distance_fraction 0.05 Minimum distance of the initial peak guesses, as fraction of the number of points. min_sigma_fraction, max_sigma_fraction 0.005, 0.3 Width bounds of Gaussian peaks, as fraction of the time range. min_peak_time_separation_fraction 1e-4 Minimum separation of the fitted peak times, as fraction of the time range. relative_intensity_upper_bounds None Optional list (one value per peak, each in (0, 1]) capping each peak's share of the total amplitude. peak_width_upper_bounds None Optional list (one value per peak) of maximum peak widths.

The peak shape is selected with the peak_shape argument of get_deconvolution ("lognormal" or "gaussian"); the peak_shape field is currently ignored.

docs.title: plotting
docs.text:
Used by the analysis plots of get_mainpeak_params (and the methods built on it) and, for figsize, by plot_heatflow_with_gradient. Measurement.plot does not use these settings.

Field Default Description figsize (10, 6) Figure size in inches, used when no ax is passed. time_unit "seconds" "seconds", "minutes" or "hours". heat_unit "W" "W" or "mW". show_plot_title True Show a title above each plot. plot_title "filename" With metadata loaded: a list of metadata column names whose values form the title, e.g. ["cement_name", "w_c"]. legend_pos "best" "best" or "outside" (right of the plot). xlims, ylims None Axis limits as (min, max) in plot units. ylims is only applied together with xlims.

docs.title: Sample-specific parameters
docs.text:
Different samples sometimes need different settings. Rules map a regular expression on the sample name to parameter overrides:

processparams.add_sample_param_rule(
    r"^c3a",  # samples whose name starts with "c3a"
    {"slope_analysis": {"first_ascending_range_method": "delta"}},
)

Rules with a higher priority are applied later and therefore win.

Warning

Sample rules are currently only honoured by get_mainpeak_params(method="ascending"). All other analyses use the base parameters for every sample.

docs.title: Reserved parameters
docs.text: The groups gradient_peakdetection, nonlin_savgol and preprocess and the field cutoff.cutoff_max exist but are not used by any analysis yet. Changing them has no effect.

docs.title: Characteristic Values
docs.text:
CaloCem extracts characteristic values from the heat flow curves. Every method returns a pandas DataFrame with one row per sample (or per peak), which can be saved with to_csv or merged with your metadata.

Quantity Method Cumulative heat at a given age get_cumulative_heat_at_hours Heat released between two times, e.g. up to the onset get_heat_between Peaks (time, height, prominence) get_peaks Minimum heat flow of the dormant period get_dormant_period_heatflow Main hydration peak: slopes, onset, peak get_mainpeak_params, see Main Peak Parameters ASTM C1679 half-maximum point get_astm_c1679_characteristics Onset by gradient threshold get_peak_onsets Peak deconvolution get_deconvolution

All examples below assume a loaded Measurement and processing parameters:

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from calocem import Measurement, ProcessingParameters

datapath = Path(__file__).parent / "calo_data"
tam = Measurement(folder=datapath, show_info=False)

processparams = ProcessingParameters()

Times are given in seconds, heat flows in W/g and heats in J/g.

docs.title: Cumulative heat
docs.text:
processparams.cutoff.cutoff_min = 0
heat_24h = tam.get_cumulative_heat_at_hours(processparams, target_h=24)

The result has the columns sample, cumulative_heat_j_g (J/g), target_h and cutoff_min.

Effect of the cutoff

The heat released before cutoff.cutoff_min is subtracted. With the default cutoff of 60 min, the result is the heat released between 1 h and target_h. Set cutoff_min = 0 to get the total heat since the start of the measurement.

Renamed in 0.4.0

get_cumulative_heat_at_hours was called get_cumulated_heat_at_hours, and cumulative_heat_j_g was called cumulated_heat_at_hours. The old method and column still work but are deprecated.

docs.title: Heat between two times
docs.text:
get_heat_between returns the heat released between start_s and end_s. The cumulative heat is interpolated at both times, and the cutoff has no effect. Each limit is either one time for all samples or one time per sample, given as a dict or pd.Series keyed by sample_short. This way you can integrate up to the onset of the main peak, which differs per sample:

onsets = tam.get_mainpeak_params(processparams).set_index("sample_short")

heat_to_onset = tam.get_heat_between(
    start_s=1800,  # 30 min
    end_s=onsets["onset_time_s_from_max_slope"],
)

The result has the columns sample, sample_short, start_s, end_s and heat_j_g (J/g). Any other time column works as well, e.g. onset_time_s_from_mean_slope, dorm_time_s or peak_time_s. The heat is NaN if a sample has no time, a time lies outside the data, or end_s is before start_s.

docs.title: Peaks
docs.text:
Peaks are searched with scipy.signal.find_peaks after the cutoff. The peakdetection parameters control the sensitivity; a smaller prominence finds smaller peaks.

processparams.cutoff.cutoff_min = 60
processparams.peakdetection.prominence = 1e-4

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
peaks = tam.get_peaks(processparams, show_plot=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100000)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.004)  # hide the initial heat flow spike
plt.show()

peaks contains the data row at each peak (time_s, normalized_heat_flow_w_g, normalized_heat_j_g, ...) plus the prominence and the number of the peak per sample (peak_nr, starting at 0). It can be exported, e.g.

peaks[["sample_short", "time_s", "normalized_heat_flow_w_g", "prominence"]].to_csv(
    "peaks.csv", index=False
)

Note

show_plot defaults to True for get_peaks. Pass show_plot=False when you only need the table.

docs.title: Dormant period
docs.text:
The dormant (induction) period is characterized by the minimum heat flow between the cutoff and the first detected peak:

dormant = tam.get_dormant_period_heatflow(processparams)

Columns: dorm_time_s, normalized_heat_flow_w_g_dormant and normalized_heat_j_g_dormant. Samples without a detected peak are missing from the result.

docs.title: Main hydration peak
docs.text:
The slopes of the main (silicate) peak and the onset of the acceleration period are determined by get_mainpeak_params:

processparams.spline_interpolation.apply = True
processparams.spline_interpolation.smoothing_1st_deriv = 1e-13
processparams.plotting.time_unit = "hours"
processparams.plotting.heat_unit = "mW"

mainpeak = tam.get_mainpeak_params(processparams, show_plot=True, plot_type="max")

It combines

  • the maximum slope: the maximum of the (smoothed) time derivative of the heat flow, with its time and value,
  • the mean slope: a tangent averaged over the ascending flank of the main peak,
  • the onset times, where these tangents intersect the dormant heat flow or the time axis,
  • the dormant period and ASTM C1679 values described on this page.

Since the derivative of measured data is noisy, smoothing (see Processing Parameters) usually improves the maximum slope. Too much smoothing flattens the peak and underestimates the slope, so compare the tangent with the curve in the plot. The Main Peak Parameters tutorial explains all options and the returned columns.

get_maximum_slope and get_average_slope return only the maximum slope or only the mean slope columns of the same analysis.

docs.title: ASTM C1679
docs.text:
The standard ASTM C1679 characterizes the main peak by the time at which the heat flow reaches half of the peak maximum on the ascending flank:

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
astm = tam.get_astm_c1679_characteristics(
    processparams, show_plot=True, xunit="h", ax=ax
)
ax.set_xlim(0, 48)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.004)
plt.show()

Columns: astm_time_s, normalized_heat_flow_w_g_astm and normalized_heat_j_g_astm. With individual=False, the half of the mean peak height of all samples is used as common threshold.

docs.title: Onset by gradient threshold
docs.text:
get_peak_onsets returns the first time at which the gradient of the heat flow exceeds gradient_threshold (in W/g/s):

onsets = tam.get_peak_onsets(gradient_threshold=1e-8, rolling=10)

Note

This method does not use the processing parameters. Data before time_discarded_s (default 900 s) is ignored instead of cutoff.cutoff_min. The default gradient_threshold of 5e-4 W/g/s is too high for typical cement pastes; values around 1e-8 W/g/s are a better starting point.

docs.title: Peak deconvolution
docs.text:
Overlapping reactions, e.g. the silicate and the aluminate peak, can be separated by fitting the heat flow after the cutoff as a sum of peaks plus a baseline:

processparams.cutoff.cutoff_min = 30
deconv = tam.get_deconvolution(
    processparams,
    n_peaks=2,
    peak_shape="lognormal",  # or "gaussian"
    baseline_mode="constant",  # "linear", "chebyshev" or "none"
    show_plot=True,
)

The result has one row per fitted component with its amplitude (W/g), peak_time_s, width, component_area (J/g) and component_area_fraction, together with the fit quality (fit_r2, fit_rmse) and the baseline coefficients. Fit settings are collected in the deconvolution parameters.

Tip

Check the plot: a component with an amplitude close to zero means that fewer peaks describe the data equally well. Its peak_time_s is then meaningless.

get_left_peak_inflection_tangent_intersection uses the fit to determine an onset of the first peak: the tangent at the inflection point of its left flank is intersected with the time axis (x_intersection_abscissa_s). Pass the result of get_deconvolution as deconvolution_results to avoid fitting twice.

docs.title: Load the Data
docs.text:
For fast reactions, e.g., reactions occurring during the first minutes of cement hydration, the thermal inertia of the calorimeter significantly broadens the heat flow signal. If the characteristic time constants are determined experimentally, a Tian correction can be applied to the heat flow data.

First we load the data.

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from calocem import Measurement, ProcessingParameters

datapath = Path(__file__).parent / "calo_data"

# load experimental data
tam = Measurement(
    folder=datapath,
    regex=r".*file1.csv",
    show_info=True,
    auto_clean=False,
    cold_start=True,
)

In the next step, we need to define a few parameters which are necessary for the Tian correction. Therefore we create a ProcessingParameters object which we call processparams in this case. The processparams object has a number of attributes which we can define. First, we define two time constants tau1 and tau2 in seconds. The numeric values need to be determined experimentally for the calorimeter. The median filter and the spline interpolation smooth the derivatives, which are otherwise very noisy (see Smoothing the Data below).

# Set Processing Parameters
processparams = ProcessingParameters()
processparams.time_constants.tau1 = 240
processparams.time_constants.tau2 = 80
processparams.median_filter.apply = True
processparams.median_filter.size = 15
processparams.spline_interpolation.apply = True
processparams.spline_interpolation.smoothing_1st_deriv = 1e-10
processparams.spline_interpolation.smoothing_2nd_deriv = 1e-10

Next we apply the Tian correction by calling the method apply_tian_correction(). We pass the processparams object defined above to the method.

# apply tian correction
tam.apply_tian_correction(
    processparams=processparams,
)

The correction adds three columns to the data: normalized_heat_flow_w_g_tian (corrected heat flow), normalized_heat_j_g_tian (heat integrated from the corrected heat flow) and gradient_normalized_heat_flow_w_g (the smoothed first derivative).

Finally, we can get the Pandas dataframe containing the calorimetric data by calling get_data(). Using the df DataFrame we can plot the calorimetry data using well-known Matplotlib methods.

df = tam.get_data()

# plot corrected and uncorrected data
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(
    df["time_s"] / 60,
    df["normalized_heat_flow_w_g"],
    linestyle="--",
    label="sample"
    )
ax.plot(
    df["time_s"] / 60,
    df["normalized_heat_flow_w_g_tian"],
    color=ax.get_lines()[-1].get_color(),
    label="Tian corrected"
    )
ax.set_xlim(0, 15)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (min)")
ax.set_ylabel("Normalized Heat Flow (W/g)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

docs.title: One or Two Tau Values
docs.text:
If only one Tau value is defined, the correction algorithm will only consider this \(\tau\) value and the data will be corrected according to

\[ P(t) = \varepsilon \left[ U(t) + \tau \frac{dU(t)}{dt} \right] \]

If two values for \(\tau\) are provided, the data will be corrected considering both values.

\[ P(t) = \varepsilon \left[ U(t) + (\tau_1+\tau_2) \frac{dU(t)}{dt} + \tau_1\tau_2 \frac{d^2U}{dt^2} \right] \]

The actual implementation of the correction algorithm is not based on the voltage \(U\) but on the heat flow. In most cases, the exported data does not contain the raw voltage data but the heat flow data which has been obtained in the instrument software with the experimentally determined value for \(\varepsilon\).

Therefore, the second equation reads like

\[ \dot{Q}_{Tian}(t) = \dot{Q}(t) + (\tau_1+\tau_2) \frac{\dot{Q}}{dt} + \tau_1\tau_2 \frac{d^2\dot{Q}}{dt^2} \]

In practical terms, if tau2 is set to None, only tau1 and the first derivative of the heat flow are considered. Note that tau2 has a default value of 100 s, so it has to be set to None explicitly.

# Set Processing Parameters
processparams = ProcessingParameters()
processparams.time_constants.tau1 = 300
processparams.time_constants.tau2 = None

The difference between having one or two tau constants can be seen in the following plot. In general, having two tau constants renders the signal even more narrow.

docs.title: No smoothing
docs.text:
It is important to smoothen the data. Otherwise, small noise in the raw heat flow data will lead to significant noise especially in the second derivative. By default the smoothing is not applied. Here, we explicitly set the attributes to False and repeat the analysis as shown above. The results demonstrates the noise in the data which originates from tiny fluctuations which result in significant noise in the second derivative.

# Set Processing Parameters
processparams.median_filter.apply = False
processparams.spline_interpolation.apply = False

docs.title: Only Median Filter
docs.text:
Here is the result of only applying a median filter with a size of 15.

# Set Processing Parameters
processparams.median_filter.apply = True
processparams.median_filter.size = 15
processparams.spline_interpolation.apply = False

docs.title: Only Spline Smoothing
docs.text:
Here is the result of only applying a Univariate Spline with smoothing of 1e-10 for both the first and the second derivative. The combination of a median filter and spline smoothing reliably delivers smooth data without introducing artifacts or significant line broadening.

# Set Processing Parameters
processparams.median_filter.apply = False
processparams.spline_interpolation.apply = True
processparams.spline_interpolation.smoothing_1st_deriv = 1e-10
processparams.spline_interpolation.smoothing_2nd_deriv = 1e-10

docs.title: Measurement
docs.text: Measurement loads the calorimetry files of a folder and provides all plotting and analysis methods. Import it with from calocem import Measurement.

docs.title: calocem.Measurement
docs.text:
Measurement(
    folder: Optional[Union[str, Path]] = None,
    show_info: bool = True,
    regex: Optional[str] = None,
    auto_clean: bool = False,
    cold_start: bool = True,
    processparams: Optional[ProcessingParameters] = None,
    new_code: Optional[bool] = None,
    processed: bool = False,
    metadata_path: Optional[Union[str, Path]] = None,
    metadata_id_column: Optional[str] = None,
    save_cache: bool = False,
)

Isothermal heat flow calorimetry data of one or more samples.

A Measurement reads all calorimetry files of a folder into one long-format DataFrame and provides methods for plotting and analysing the samples.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default folder str or Path

Folder with the exported calorimetry files (.csv or .xls). Subfolders are not searched. If None, an empty Measurement is created.

None show_info bool

Print information while loading, by default True.

True regex str

Regular expression matched against the beginning of the file names; only matching files are loaded.

None auto_clean bool

Drop rows without heat flow values and merge differently named temperature columns into temperature_c, by default False.

False cold_start bool

If True (default), read the files. If False, read _data.pickle and _info.pickle from the current working directory instead (see save_cache).

True processparams ProcessingParameters

Default processing parameters for all analysis methods. The downsample settings are applied while loading.

None new_code bool

Deprecated, has no effect.

None processed bool

Read plain CSV files previously written from :meth:get_data, by default False.

False metadata_path str or Path

CSV or Excel file with one row of metadata per sample, see :meth:add_metadata_source.

None metadata_id_column str

Column of the metadata file holding the sample names. Required together with metadata_path.

None save_cache bool

Write _data.pickle and _info.pickle to the current working directory after loading, by default False. Prefer :meth:save.

False

Raises:

Type Description AutoCleanException

If auto_clean fails.

ColdStartException

If cold_start=False and no cache files are found.

Examples:

get_mainpeak_params(
    processparams: Optional[ProcessingParameters] = None,
    target_col: str = "normalized_heat_flow_w_g",
    age_col: str = "time_s",
    show_plot: bool = False,
    save_plot: bool = False,
    plot_type: str = "mean",
    regex: Optional[str] = None,
    plotpath: Optional[Path] = None,
    ax=None,
    method: str = "mean",
    monochrome: bool = False,
    marker_size: float = 1.0,
) -> pd.DataFrame

Characterize the main hydration peak: slopes, onset times and peak values.

With method="mean" (default) two analyses are combined:

  • maximum slope: the maximum of the time derivative of the heat flow (after optional smoothing), and the onset where the tangent at this point meets the dormant heat flow or the time axis;
  • mean slope: a tangent averaged over the ascending flank between slope_analysis.flank_fraction_start and flank_fraction_end of the peak height, and its onset.

With method="ascending" the slope of the first ascending segment up to a threshold (slope_analysis.first_ascending_*) is determined instead. This is the only analysis that honours sample parameter rules.

In both cases the dormant period (:meth:get_dormant_period_heatflow) and ASTM C1679 (:meth:get_astm_c1679_characteristics) values are added.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default processparams ProcessingParameters

Processing parameters. If None, the parameters of the Measurement are used.

None target_col str

Column with the heat flow, by default "normalized_heat_flow_w_g".

'normalized_heat_flow_w_g' age_col str

Column with the time in seconds, by default "time_s".

'time_s' show_plot bool

Plot the analysis for each sample, by default False.

False save_plot bool

Save each plot as PNG to plotpath, by default False.

False plot_type str

For method="mean": show the "mean" (default) or "max" slope analysis.

'mean' regex str

Regular expression; only samples whose name matches are analysed.

None plotpath Path

Folder for save_plot.

None ax Axes

Axes to draw into. If None, one figure per sample is created and shown.

None method str

"mean" (default) or "ascending".

'mean' monochrome bool

Draw all markers in black, by default False.

False marker_size float

Scale factor for marker sizes, by default 1.0.

1.0

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

One row per sample. For method="mean" the columns include gradient_from_max_slope (W/g/s), max_slope_time_s, onset_time_s_from_max_slope, onset_time_min_max_slope, gradient_of_mean_slope (W/g/s), mean_slope_time_s, onset_time_s_from_mean_slope, peak_time_s, normalized_heat_flow_w_g_at_peak, dorm_time_s, normalized_heat_flow_w_g_dormant and astm_time_s, together with the heat flows and heats at these times. For method="ascending" the slope is in gradient_of_first_ascending_slope_to_fraction_of_max and the onset in onset_time_s_from_first_ascending_slope.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If method is not "mean" or "ascending".

Examples:

>>> processparams = ProcessingParameters()
>>> processparams.spline_interpolation.apply = True
>>> result = tam.get_mainpeak_params(processparams, show_plot=True, plot_type="max")
>>> result[["sample_short", "gradient_from_max_slope", "onset_time_s_from_max_slope"]]

docs.title: apply_tian_correction
docs.text:
apply_tian_correction(
    processparams: Optional[ProcessingParameters] = None,
) -> None

Apply Tian correction to the heat flow data.

Corrects the measured heat flow for the thermal inertia of the calorimeter using one or two time constants (tau1, tau2) from processparams.

Single time constant (tau2 = None): hf_corrected = dHF/dt * tau1 + HF

Dual time constants: hf_corrected = dHF/dt * (tau1 + tau2) + d²HF/dt² * tau1*tau2 + HF

Results are written to three new columns: - normalized_heat_flow_w_g_tian - gradient_normalized_heat_flow_w_g - normalized_heat_j_g_tian

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default processparams ProcessingParameters

Processing parameters containing time_constants.tau1 and time_constants.tau2. Uses instance processparams if not provided.
